DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
# Review: Menu Pricing Review, Spring 2026

**Overall:** The arithmetic in the document is correct as far as it goes. The £810/week figure and the margin column in Table 1 both check out. But four of the author's headline claims don't survive a check against the document's own data. The most serious problem is that the risotto has the **highest** margin on the menu, not the weakest. The other three: the projection ignores the beef increase reported in the same paper, the projected gross profit likely includes VAT, and the 71% margin would not happen. Once these are corrected, the price increases still help, but by roughly a quarter to half of the stated £42k. The risotto swap, as proposed, lowers profit.

## Major issues

### 1. The risotto has the best margin, not the weakest
From Table 1:

| Dish | Margin | GP per plate |
|---|---|---|
| Mushroom risotto | **80%** (highest) | £11.20 |
| Chicken curry | 75% | £10.90 |
| Beef burger | 72% | £10.80 |
| Fish and chips | 69% | £11.40 |
| Sirloin steak | 60% (lowest) | £15.60 |
| Specials | 64% | – |

Its sales of 90 plates are joint-lowest with specials, not uniquely lowest. Replacing it with a "seasonal vegetarian special at the same price" swaps an 80% dish for a category that averages 64%. On 90 plates at £14, that costs about **£200/week** in gross profit, unless the new special is costed to match the risotto's margin.

The case for removing the risotto, if there is one, would rest on its low popularity, not its profitability. It may also be the only fixed vegetarian main. The proposal should be reworded, or the swap made conditional on the special hitting a margin target.

### 2. The projection ignores the 12% beef increase
Section 4 reports the rise, but section 5.3 leaves it out. Assuming the whole food cost of each dish is beef, which is an upper bound since the burger cost includes the bun and sides:

- Burger: £4.20 → £4.70, which is +£0.50 × 260 = about **£131/week**
- Steak: £10.40 → £11.65, which is +£1.25 × 120 = about **£150/week**

That is roughly **£280/week** of extra cost. Once it's included, both beef dishes end up with **lower** margins than today, even at the new prices:

| Dish | Margin now | Margin at new price |
|---|---|---|
| Burger | 72% | about 70.6% |
| Steak | 60% | about 58.4% |

In margin terms, the steak increase doesn't even cover its own cost rise.

### 3. VAT probably isn't accounted for
UK menu prices include 20% VAT. If the gross margins and the £810 are calculated on VAT-inclusive prices, as they appear to be, then:
- The extra revenue the business keeps is £810 ÷ 1.2 = **£675/week**.
- All the margins are overstated. Fish and chips is about 63% ex-VAT, not 69%.

If the 70% target is measured ex-VAT, as it normally would be, the paper compares figures calculated on different bases. Either way, the paper should state which basis it uses.

### 4. The corrected profit and margin are much lower
Combining the above, and assuming volumes hold:

| | Per week | Per year |
|---|---|---|
| Stated | £810 | £42,120 |
| Less beef increase | about £530 | about £27,500 |
| Also ex-VAT | about £395 | about £20,500 |
| Also the risotto swap at 64% | about £190 | about £10,000 |

The ~71% main-course margin also falls away. I estimated specials at an average of £15, since the paper gives no price. On that basis:
- Main-course margin today is about 69.4% (VAT-inclusive basis).
- The price increases alone take it to about 71%, which matches the paper's figure.
- With the beef rise as well, it is about 69.2%.
- With the risotto swap too, it is about 68.1%, below today's level.

Even a full 71% on mains wouldn't by itself "restore our 70% overall target." That target covers all courses, and the paper doesn't examine starters or desserts.

## Other weaknesses

5. **"Remain the value option" isn't quite true.** Each new price is below the midpoint of its competitor range, so that claim holds: £17.50 vs £17.98, £16.00 vs £16.50, £28.00 vs £29.50. But we are currently the *cheapest* on all three dishes, and after the change all three are above the cheapest competitor: £17.50 vs £16.95, £16.00 vs £15.50, £28.00 vs £27.00. We'd move from lowest to mid-low.

6. **Repeat bookings don't show that customers will accept higher prices.** The 60% figure is a share of *bookings*, so walk-ins are excluded. Regulars are also the guests most likely to notice the increase, which section 7 concedes. The claim that the 2024 change had "no visible effect" is anecdotal. A quick before-and-after look at covers would make it evidence.

7. **There's no sensitivity analysis.** "If volumes hold" is the whole case, so the paper should show break-even volumes. For example, fish and chips GP per plate goes from £11.40 to £12.40, so a volume loss of about 8% on that dish cancels its gain.

8. **The monitoring plan will give misleading results.** Comparing April–May to a January–February baseline mixes the price effect with seasonality. Spring trade, including Easter, which falls on 5 April 2026, is normally stronger, so falling demand could be hidden. Better comparisons would be:
   - the same weeks last year, or
   - the unchanged dishes (curry and specials) as a control.

   The plan also needs a trigger: what drop, over what period, leads to what action.

9. **The claim about lunch is unsupported.** Weekday lunch is described as "a small share," but no figures are given. All the paper says is that Friday and Saturday dinner is just under half of sales, which leaves more than half spread across the other services.

10. **Factual error in section 8.** The restaurant opens Wednesday to Sunday, which is **five** trading days, not six. The annual figure also multiplies by 52 weeks, with no allowance for closures.

11. **The author's framing overstates the evidence.**
    - "Every main course": specials are reported only as a group.
    - "Full competitor price check": only three dishes were compared, with nothing on the curry or risotto.

## Suggested fixes before this goes to the owners

1. **Correct the risotto rationale.** Either keep it, or make its replacement conditional on a special costed at a margin of 75% or more.
2. **Recompute section 5.3** with the beef increase included, on a stated VAT basis, and add a simple break-even volume table.
3. **Reconsider the steak.** Something nearer £29 restores its current margin after the beef rise and stays under the competitor midpoint of £29.50.
4. **Restate the margin outcome** honestly, and note that reaching the 70% food target needs action beyond mains.
5. **Fix the monitoring plan** with a seasonal comparison and a defined action threshold.
6. **Correct "six trading days"** to five.

The core proposal, a modest price rise on the three highest-volume dishes, is still sensible. Prices haven't moved since September 2024 and costs are rising. The paper just needs to present a smaller, honest benefit instead of £42k.
